title: Twenty-two years: 14 October 2004 remembered
author: Editorial Desk
summary: Twenty-two years after 14 October 2004: what Dattopant Thengadi built, how he lived, and questions his work leaves for today's karyakartas.
body:
*Photo: Dattopant Thengadi*

On **14 October 2026**, twenty-two years have passed since **Dattopant Thengadi**, the founder of Bharatiya Mazdoor Sangh, passed away at Pune. Anniversaries of this kind are easy to mark with a garland and a speech. This post tries to do something slightly harder: to look at what he built, how he lived, and what questions his work leaves for the people who now carry it forward.

## A life in brief

Dattatreya Bapurao Thengadi, known as Dattopant, was born on 10 November 1920 at Arvi in Wardha district, Maharashtra. He studied law at Nagpur, and from 1942 he worked as a full-time pracharak of the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh, a role he kept until his death. He died at Pune on 14 October 2004 ([Wikipedia: Dattopant Thengadi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dattopant_Thengadi)). A tribute on the Thengadi archive records that he died at Deendayal Hospital in Pune ([Dattopant Thengadi Archive](https://dbthengadi.in/remembering-shradheya-dattopant-thengadi/)). He sat in the Rajya Sabha for two terms, from 1964 to 1976, and wrote on labour, economics and national reconstruction in Hindi, Marathi and English.

## What stands today

The first and largest part of his legacy is Bharatiya Mazdoor Sangh itself. BMS was founded on 23 July 1955, the birth anniversary of Lokmanya Tilak, at a gathering in Bhopal under his leadership. It was not born from a split in an existing union, so it started with no members, no office, no funds and no experience. It was conceived as a trade union rooted in nationalism and kept apart from party politics ([VVGNLI: BMS at a Glance](https://vvgnli.gov.in/sites/default/files/Bharatiya%20Mazdoor%20Sangh%20At%20a%20Glance.pdf)). Its first All India conference, held in Delhi in 1967, brought together 541 affiliated unions with about 246,000 members. After Government verification, it was declared the second-largest central trade union in 1984 with 1,211,355 members, and in 1996 the Ministry of Labour declared it the largest, with 3,117,324 members on the verification reckoning date of 31 December 1989 ([VVGNLI: BMS at a Glance](https://vvgnli.gov.in/sites/default/files/Bharatiya%20Mazdoor%20Sangh%20At%20a%20Glance.pdf)). Those figures are historical, and readers should check the latest verification results, but they show how a union that began with nothing was built from the ground up.

Beyond BMS, he is associated with the founding or co-founding of a series of other organisations: the Bharatiya Kisan Sangh in 1979, the Swadeshi Jagaran Manch, the Samajik Samarasata Manch, the Paryavaran Manch, and the Akhil Bharatiya Vidyarthi Parishad, Akhil Bharatiya Adhivakta Parishad, Akhil Bharatiya Grahak Panchayat and Bharatiya Vichara Kendra as co-founder ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dattopant_Thengadi)). Within the BMS family, the BMS pamphlet lists the Bharatiya Shram-Shodh Mandal, a research body founded on 26 May 1980; the Vishwakarma Shramik Shiksha Sanstha, a labour training institute at Nagpur; the Sarva Panth Samadar Manch, founded in 1994; and the monthly journals *Vishwakarma Chetna* in Hindi and *Vishwakarma Sanket* in English. The head office of BMS in New Delhi carries his name, Dattopant Thengadi Bhawan, as the BMS website notes ([BMS website](https://www.bms.org.in/?p=388)).

## How he lived

Reports of his life stress simplicity. The journalist S. Gurumurthy, in a tribute written weeks after his death, described him as someone who owned no house, car or phone, lived in a small room provided by the organisation in Delhi, never married, and travelled by overnight bus and mostly second-class train. Gurumurthy wrote that he rarely appeared in public, did not like to be photographed or interviewed, and that national newspapers hardly noticed his death ([Gurumurthy, "A Tapasvi dies. Unnoticed"](https://dbthengadi.in/dattopant-thengadi-a-tapasvi-dies-unnoticed/)). These are one author's recollections, but they match the accounts of others on the Thengadi archive, which also records that he declined the Padma Bhushan offered by the Government of the day ([Dattopant Thengadi Archive](https://dbthengadi.in/remembering-shradheya-dattopant-thengadi/)).

The same archive notes that he was willing to criticise whichever Government was in office. It records that he criticised the farm and labour policies of the then NDA Government as well as the stand of the Congress-led Government on global trade. For a union that insists on being independent of political parties, that habit of speaking on the merits matters.

## The ideas he left

Several ideas run through BMS's work, and they can be traced to his writing and speeches:

- **Nation first, then industry, then the worker.** The Hindi slogan *Rashtra hit, Udyog hit, Mazdoor hit* is often used by BMS to express this order of concern. The BMS website also lists the motto "Nationalise the Labour, Labourise the Industry, Industrialise the Nation" ([BMS website](https://www.bms.org.in/?p=388)).
- **Labourisation.** The BMS pamphlet describes labourisation as workers collectively owning and managing units, and cites the New Central Jute Mills in West Bengal as an example.
- **The industrial family.** Rejecting the class-struggle theory, BMS speaks of workers, managers and owners as members of one family who must settle differences by dialogue.
- **The worker as consumer and citizen.** In his 1986 booklet *Consumer: A Sovereign without Sovereignty*, prepared for the first All India Study Class of the Akhil Bharatiya Grahak Panchayat, he argued that consumer "sovereignty" is largely theoretical in India. He wrote that peasants, workers and consumers are all exploited through middlemen and profiteering, and that their interests are not opposed ([Thengadi, Consumer: A Sovereign without Sovereignty](https://vvgnli.gov.in/sites/default/files/Consumer%20A%20Sovereign%20without%20Sovereignty.pdf)).
- **Swadeshi.** The pamphlet states that BMS promotes swadeshi products and a self-reliant economy.

## Questions for today

It would be wrong to put words into his mouth, so these are our questions, not his. They are the ones any BMS unit might ask of itself on this day.

- Are **workers educated** about their rights and duties, and do they know what the Labour Codes now say?
- Is the union's **money and work** handled with openness and honesty, with accounts shown to members?
- Are the **youngest karyakartas** being prepared, not merely used, so that leadership has successors?
- Is the **worker in the smallest unit**, the contract worker, the scheme worker, the gig worker, heard as clearly as the worker in the largest plant?
- Does the union speak on the **merits of a policy**, whoever has proposed it?

## A reading list

For those who want to go to the source, the Thengadi archive hosts a catalogue of his books and booklets in Hindi, Marathi and English, including *The Perspective*, *Third Way* and *Labour Policy*, together with tributes by other writers ([Dattopant Thengadi Archive](https://dbthengadi.in)). The history *The Onward March of BMS* is also available online ([The Onward March of BMS](https://cdn.dbthengadi.in/scan/The_Onward_March_OF_BMS.pdf)).

## A practical tribute

Hold a small study circle in your union this month. Choose a short passage, perhaps ten pages, from one of his books or from the BMS history. Read it aloud, discuss for half an hour how it applies to a problem in your own workplace, and write down one action to take before the next meeting. A tribute that ends in an action is closer to the way he worked than a ceremony that ends in applause.
